protocol.name: rill_stream_v1
protocol.copyright: Rill command-stream protocol (specs/wgpu-renderer.md W4/D4). MIT OR Apache-2.0.
protocol.description: Lets a client deliver its window content as a Rill DrawCommand stream (the rill_ui::stream binary encoding) instead of a pixel buffer. The surface stays an ordinary xdg_toplevel for window management; only the content path changes. Frames are passed as memfds (the wl_shm bulk pattern) and latch on wl_surface.commit, so a frame and the surface state it belongs to are one atomic transaction.

interface.name: rill_stream_manager_v1
interface.description:
Global for turning a wl_surface into a vector-native surface.
Version 2 adds rill_stream_v1.attach_image. The version lives here as well as on the stream because a stream inherits the version of the manager that created it — a v1 manager can only ever make a v1 stream, whatever the stream interface itself declares.

entry.name: stream_exists
entry.summary: the surface already has a stream object

request.name: get_stream

description.summary: create a stream for a surface

request.description: Bind a command stream to the surface. One stream per surface.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Existing stream objects survive the manager.

interface.name: rill_stream_v1
interface.description:
Carries encoded DrawCommand frames for one surface, and the raster images those frames refer to.
A frame names an image by its source string and never carries its pixels: a command stream is kilobytes and stays kilobytes, which is the whole reason it exists. Pixels travel out of band, once per source, through attach_image — the same sealed-memfd handoff a frame uses, on the same connection, bound to the same surface.
The client resolves images, not the compositor. It already must: the layout box comes from the image's natural size, so the client has fetched and decoded the image before it can emit a frame mentioning it. Resolving them a second time in the compositor would need credentials the compositor does not have and should not be given — it would be a desktop-wide deputy that any client could aim at any path by naming it in a document, and the render-or-placeholder outcome would report whether that path exists.

entry.name: invalid_stream
entry.summary: the attached bytes failed strict decoding

entry.name: oversized
entry.summary: the attached frame exceeds the stream size cap

entry.name: image_malformed
entry.summary: image size does not match width * height * 4

entry.name: image_budget
entry.summary: the surface's image memory budget is exhausted

request.name: attach
request.description: Stage an encoded frame. The fd is read immediately (size bytes); the frame becomes the surface content on the next wl_surface.commit. width and height are the logical size the frame was laid out for.

request.name: attach_image

description.summary: supply the pixels for one image source

request.description:
Give the compositor the decoded pixels behind one image source, so that DrawCommand::Image referring to `source` paints rather than showing the placeholder box.
`fd` holds raw RGBA8, top-left origin, tightly packed: `size` must equal width * height * 4 exactly, or the compositor raises image_malformed. Raw, not an encoded format, deliberately — the compositor decoding client-supplied PNGs would put an image codec on the path of untrusted bytes, and the client has the decoded pixels already.
`source` is the same string the frame's Image command carries, and is scoped to this stream: two surfaces naming "/logo.png" are naming their own, which is right, because they may be talking to different servers.
Sent once per source, not per frame. The compositor uploads the pixels to a texture and drops the CPU copy; the client may then drop its own. Re-attaching the same source replaces it — that is how an image that changed is updated.
Images are held against a per-surface byte budget. When it is reached the compositor releases images the current frame does not name, least recently used first, and says so with image_released. image_budget is raised only when even that is not enough — a single frame naming more pixels than the budget allows. All of a surface's images are released when its stream is destroyed.

event.name: image_released

description.summary: an image is gone and must be sent again to reappear

event.description:
The compositor has dropped the pixels for `source`. A frame naming it now paints the placeholder box until the client attaches it again.
This is what makes the budget survivable. Without it the choice at the cap is between refusing new images — so a window that browses enough pictures stops showing them permanently — and evicting silently, which is a picture that vanishes and never returns. A client that hears this simply forgets having sent it, and the next frame that needs it sends it again.
Only images the current frame does not name are released, so this does not arrive for something on screen and cannot become a release/re-attach loop.

request.name: set_tier

description.summary: classify what this surface shows from now on

request.description:
The sensitivity tier the surface's content records at in the semantic history, as the shown document declared it (specs/history.md decision 4: the document is the app's only channel to its viewer; this request is the client→compositor leg).
Latched with the next attach: the tier applies to that frame and every one after it, until changed. Send before the frame it classifies — a tier that arrives after the frame has classified the wrong content.
`tier` is the closed set the history format knows (0 routine, 1 sensitive, 2 sealed). A value outside it raises invalid_stream: an unknown-but-higher tier must fail closed, never record as routine.
The fail-closed rule binds both ends. A client whose document declares a tier and whose compositor predates this request must not attach the frame at all — sending it would record classified content at tier 0, which is the exact failure this request exists to prevent.

request.name: destroy
request.description: The surface reverts to ordinary buffer content.
